column1: # Tool|Title|Evidence|Cause|Investigate|Repair|Verify|Prevent

Bash|The false green light|A backup command fails, but its script ends with echo success and exits zero.|The final successful command masks the earlier failure.|Inspect exit codes and error handling around the backup command.|Explicitly check the backup exit code and return a nonzero status on failure.|Simulate a backup failure and confirm the job is marked failed.|Add failure-path checks and explicit error handling to backup scripts.

Python|The missing package|A job imports requests successfully in a shell but fails in its virtual environment.|The job environment lacks a dependency installed in a different interpreter.|Compare the job interpreter and its installed packages with the interactive shell.|Install pinned dependencies into the interpreter environment used by the job.|Run the job using its actual interpreter and confirm the import succeeds.|Create reproducible virtual environments from a committed dependency file.

GitHub|The blocked merge|The required check is waiting forever; the workflow only runs on pushes to main.|The required workflow never runs on pull requests.|Inspect workflow event triggers and the exact required check name.|Configure the required check to run on relevant pull requests.|Open a trial pull request and confirm the named check reports a result.|Validate required checks against workflow triggers when changing branch policies.

Nginx|The dead upstream|Nginx returns 502; its error log shows connection refused to 127.0.0.1:9000; the app listens on 9001.|The reverse proxy targets the wrong upstream port.|Compare the loaded upstream configuration with the application's listening socket.|Correct the upstream port, validate Nginx configuration, then reload.|Send a request through the proxy and confirm the expected application response.|Keep upstream endpoints in version-controlled configuration with deployment checks.

Apache HTTP Server|The closed virtual host|Only one Apache site returns 403; its directory rule says Require all denied.|The virtual host explicitly denies directory access.|Inspect the matched virtual host and its effective directory authorization rules.|Replace the unintended deny rule with the intended restricted access policy.|Request the site as an allowed client and confirm denied clients remain blocked.|Review virtual-host authorization changes and check allowed and denied paths.

HAProxy|The empty backend|HAProxy marks every server down after the health path changed from /health to /ready.|The proxy health check requests a removed endpoint.|Compare health-check configuration with the backend's current readiness endpoint.|Update the health-check path to the intended supported readiness endpoint.|Confirm backends become healthy and requests route successfully.|Version the health-check contract alongside application endpoint changes.

DNS|The old address|The authoritative DNS server returns the new IP; a recursive resolver returns the old IP with remaining TTL.|A recursive resolver is still serving a valid cached answer.|Compare authoritative and recursive answers and their TTLs.|Wait for the valid cache TTL or use an approved controlled resolver cache refresh.|Confirm the affected resolver returns the new address after cache expiration.|Lower TTL ahead of planned migrations and allow time for old TTLs to expire.

TLS|The broken chain|A TLS client trusts the root CA but fails verification; the server sends only its leaf certificate.|The server omits a required intermediate certificate.|Inspect the presented chain with a TLS client using server name indication.|Configure the server to present the appropriate intermediate certificate chain.|Verify the hostname and chain using a clean client trust store.|Validate deployed certificate chains automatically after renewals.

systemd|The restart loop|A systemd unit exits with status 203/EXEC; ExecStart points to a missing executable.|The service unit references an invalid executable path.|Check ExecStart and whether the referenced executable exists and is executable.|Correct the service executable path, reload unit configuration and start the service.|Confirm the unit stays active and its application health endpoint succeeds.|Validate service unit paths against packaged artifacts before deployment.

Docker Compose|The lonely database|An app in Compose connects to localhost:5432; PostgreSQL runs in the separate db service.|Inside the app container, localhost points to the app container itself.|Inspect the connection URL and the Compose service network names.|Use the db service name and container port in the app connection URL.|Run a database connection check from the app service.|Use service discovery names and document container versus host networking.

Podman|The unreadable mount|A rootless Podman container cannot read a bind mount on an enforcing SELinux host; audit logs show label denials.|The bind mount has a host label incompatible with container access.|Inspect SELinux audit denials and the ownership and label of the mount.|Apply the appropriate approved container label for the mount, using :Z for a private mount when suitable.|Confirm the container reads the mount while SELinux stays enforcing.|Document volume label and user-namespace ownership requirements.

BuildKit|The vanished build context|A Dockerfile copies dist/, but .dockerignore excludes dist/ from the build context.|The required artifact is excluded before the build reaches COPY.|Compare the build context, .dockerignore patterns and the COPY source.|Include the required build artifact in the context or build it in a suitable stage.|Build from a clean checkout and confirm the image contains the artifact.|Check build-context rules whenever adding new generated assets.

Amazon ECR|The expired pull credential|A node reports registry authentication failure; its manually generated ECR login was created yesterday.|The manually stored ECR authorization token has expired.|Check the registry credential source and token generation time.|Refresh the token through the approved identity flow or restore the platform credential provider.|Pull the intended image using the actual workload identity path.|Use automatic short-lived registry authentication rather than a static token.

GitHub Container Registry|The invisible image|A workflow can access its repository, but pushing a package fails with a packages write permission error.|The workflow token lacks package publishing permission.|Inspect workflow token permissions and package access rules.|Grant the publishing job the narrowly scoped packages write permission it requires.|Run the publish job and verify the expected immutable image digest exists.|Declare minimal job-level token permissions explicitly.

Jenkins|The vanished agent|A Jenkins job is queued with label docker-builder; no online agent has that label.|The job's agent label has no available matching executor.|Inspect agent labels, online status and executor availability.|Restore the intended agent or correct the label to an approved compatible agent.|Confirm the job runs on the intended agent and completes its build.|Monitor agent availability and keep agent labels under configuration control.

GitHub Actions|The missing deployment identity|A workflow's cloud login reports that it cannot request an OIDC token; its token permissions omit id-token write.|The job is not permitted to request the OIDC identity token.|Inspect job token permissions and the cloud login action's OIDC requirements.|Grant id-token write to the deployment job and retain narrowly scoped cloud trust.|Confirm OIDC exchange succeeds only for the intended repository and environment.|Use explicit OIDC permissions and environment-bound cloud trust policies.

GitLab CI|The protected variable|A deployment on an unprotected feature branch sees an empty protected credential variable.|Protected CI variables are withheld from the unprotected branch context.|Inspect branch protection, variable protection and pipeline source.|Run deployment from the intended protected context rather than exposing the variable broadly.|Confirm the protected deployment gets its credential and feature branches do not.|Separate trusted deployment pipelines from untrusted branch jobs.

Azure DevOps|The locked environment|A release completed build stages but waits at an environment approval check.|The deployment environment requires an approval that has not been granted.|Inspect environment checks and the identity of the required approver.|Request the configured approval through the environment's review process.|Confirm the deployment starts after a legitimate recorded approval.|Document release approvers and maintain a clear approval escalation process.

CircleCI|The unavailable context|A CircleCI job fails before deployment because the triggering actor is outside the restricted context group.|The actor is not authorized to use the deployment context.|Inspect the context's security restrictions and triggering actor membership.|Run the deployment through an authorized identity or approved group access change.|Confirm an authorized deployment receives the context while unauthorized jobs remain blocked.|Review context memberships and document trusted deployment identities.

Maven|The incompatible bytecode|A Maven service compiled for Java 21 runs on Java 17 and reports UnsupportedClassVersionError.|The runtime Java version is older than the compiled bytecode target.|Compare compiler release settings with the deployed Java runtime version.|Align the supported runtime and compiler target, then rebuild or redeploy accordingly.|Start the built artifact using the intended production Java runtime.|Pin and validate compatible build and runtime JDK versions.

Gradle|The inconsistent build tool|A Gradle build succeeds locally but CI uses a different globally installed Gradle release.|CI bypasses the project's pinned Gradle wrapper.|Compare the CI invocation with the committed wrapper version.|Use the reviewed project Gradle wrapper in CI.|Build a clean checkout with the wrapper in both local and CI environments.|Pin the wrapper and review wrapper distribution changes.

npm|The moving dependency tree|CI uses npm install without a committed lockfile and produces different dependency versions on different days.|Dependency resolution is not locked to a reproducible tree.|Inspect the lockfile and the dependency installation command.|Commit a reviewed lockfile and use npm ci for reproducible installation.|Install from a clean checkout and confirm the lockfile-defined tree is used.|Review dependency and lockfile updates together in pull requests.

Nexus Repository|The denied release|A Nexus release repository rejects deployment of an existing version under a no-redeploy policy.|The pipeline attempts to overwrite an immutable published release.|Inspect the artifact coordinates, existing version and deployment policy.|Publish a new release version instead of overwriting the existing immutable artifact.|Resolve both versions and verify their distinct coordinates and checksums.|Enforce unique release versions and promote immutable artifacts.

JFrog Artifactory|The rejected upload|Artifactory rejects a publish job; the service token is valid but lacks deploy permission on the target repository.|The publishing identity lacks the repository's deploy permission.|Inspect the token identity, target repository and effective permission target.|Grant only the required deploy permission to the publishing identity.|Publish a trial artifact to the approved location without broadening unrelated access.|Maintain repository-specific service identities and review permissions as code.

Terraform|The locked blueprint|Terraform reports a remote state lock owned by an active pipeline that is still applying changes.|Another legitimate apply currently owns the state lock.|Inspect the lock owner and the active pipeline before changing the lock.|Wait for the legitimate apply and serialize subsequent runs.|Confirm the first apply finishes and a later plan acquires the lock normally.|Use one coordinated writer per state and pipeline concurrency controls.

OpenTofu|The wrong workspace|An OpenTofu plan proposes staging infrastructure while the operator intended production; the selected workspace is staging.|The operator selected the wrong workspace for the intended change.|Inspect the workspace, backend and variable set before applying.|Select the intended workspace and reviewed variable set, then regenerate the plan.|Review resource names and scope in the new plan before approval.|Add explicit environment identity checks and approvals before applies.

AWS CloudFormation|The impossible export deletion|A stack update fails because another stack imports an output scheduled for removal.|A dependent stack still consumes the exported output.|List the export's importing stacks and inspect their references.|Migrate consumers away from the export before removing it.|Confirm there are no remaining imports, then update the producer stack.|Model cross-stack dependencies and use staged contract migrations.

Pulumi|The unreachable state|Pulumi login targets the wrong backend URL, so the expected stack cannot be found.|The CLI is using a different state backend from the team.|Compare the active backend URL and stack organization with team configuration.|Select the approved backend and exact existing stack rather than creating a replacement.|Preview the expected stack and confirm its resource identities match reality.|Pin backend and organization selection in deployment configuration.

Ansible|The repeated change|An Ansible shell task appends the same config line on every run and always reports changed.|A non-idempotent shell operation duplicates configuration.|Inspect the task and compare the target file across repeated runs.|Use an idempotent module such as lineinfile with the intended matching rule.|Run the playbook twice and confirm the second run makes no change.|Prefer declarative modules and check repeat-run behavior in configuration reviews.

Packer|The unreachable image builder|A Packer builder launches in a private subnet with no route from its runner to the SSH address.|The runner cannot reach the builder's selected SSH network path.|Inspect runner location, builder address selection, routes and security groups.|Use an approved reachable private build path or configured bastion access.|Confirm the runner establishes SSH over the intended restricted route.|Design image-build networking explicitly and avoid accidental public exposure.

AWS IAM|The invisible deny|An IAM role has an identity-policy allow, but the request is blocked by an explicit organization SCP deny.|An explicit organization policy deny overrides the identity-policy allow.|Inspect the evaluated organization policies and request context.|Seek an approved narrowly scoped policy adjustment or use a permitted operation.|Repeat the exact request and confirm unrelated restrictions remain enforced.|Include organization policy evaluation when reviewing access changes.

Amazon EC2|The inaccessible host|An EC2 host is healthy; SSH times out; its security group allows a different source IP than the administrator's current IP.|The SSH ingress rule does not permit the actual client source.|Compare the current client source with the instance security-group ingress rules.|Use the approved access method or narrowly update the authorized source rule.|Connect using the intended access path and confirm other sources remain blocked.|Prefer managed access and documented restricted administrative ingress.

Amazon VPC|The stranded private subnet|A private instance cannot reach the Internet; its subnet route table has no default route to the existing NAT gateway.|The private subnet lacks its intended outbound default route.|Inspect the effective route table and the NAT gateway's availability and public routing.|Add the approved default route to the available NAT gateway for that subnet.|Verify outbound connectivity without exposing unsolicited inbound access.|Manage subnet routes as code and validate outbound connectivity per subnet.

AWS ALB|The unhealthy target|An ALB checks port 80 but the target application serves readiness on port 8080.|The target group's health-check port does not match the application.|Compare target registration, health-check port and application listening port.|Correct the health-check port and retain the required restricted security-group path.|Confirm target health becomes healthy and requests succeed through the ALB.|Validate target-group checks against the deployed application contract.

AWS Auto Scaling|The capped fleet|An Auto Scaling group wants eight instances but max size is four; metrics show sustained CPU pressure.|The group's maximum capacity prevents the intended scale-out.|Inspect desired and maximum capacity, scaling activities and account quotas.|Raise the approved maximum after confirming quotas, budget and downstream capacity.|Confirm new instances become healthy and load per instance falls.|Capacity-plan autoscaling limits and alert when the group reaches its ceiling.

Amazon S3|The blocked public object|An S3 bucket policy allows public reads, but effective Block Public Access prevents public access by design.|The effective public-access block overrides the intended public policy behavior.|Inspect bucket and account public-access blocks and the intended delivery design.|Use approved private delivery such as CloudFront with origin access rather than broadly removing protection.|Confirm authorized delivery succeeds while direct unauthorized bucket access remains denied.|Keep buckets private by default and review public delivery architecture explicitly.

Amazon RDS|The exhausted connection budget|RDS rejects new connections; current connections are at the configured limit; application pools grew after scaling out.|Aggregate application connection pools exceed the database connection budget.|Compare active connections, per-instance pool limits and application replica count.|Reduce or bound aggregate pool usage and handle queued requests safely.|Verify connections stay below the safe limit and transaction latency recovers.|Budget database connections across replicas and use appropriate pooling or proxying.

Amazon Route 53|The failing probe|Route 53 health checks fail; the app responds locally but firewall logs show probe source addresses denied.|The health-check probes are blocked at the network boundary.|Inspect the health-check endpoint and firewall denies for the documented probe sources.|Permit the required approved health-check traffic to the correct endpoint.|Confirm health-check status recovers and traffic policies behave as intended.|Track provider probe-network changes and validate external checks.

AWS Lambda|The runaway concurrency|A Lambda function cannot open new database sessions during a burst; each concurrent invocation opens a fresh connection.|Unbounded function concurrency overwhelms the database connection capacity.|Correlate function concurrency with database connection count and pool behavior.|Bound concurrency and introduce suitable connection reuse or a managed proxy.|Load-test within approved limits and confirm stable connections and latency.|Set concurrency budgets based on downstream capacity and monitor saturation.

Amazon CloudWatch|The silent alarm|CloudWatch shows the metric in one region, but the alarm watches a different region and receives no data.|The alarm is configured in the wrong region for the metric.|Compare the alarm region, namespace and dimensions with the emitted metric.|Create or correct the alarm in the region containing the intended metric.|Trigger a controlled metric condition and verify the alarm transition and notification.|Validate alarm region and dimensions alongside the emitting workload.

Amazon EKS|The unauthorized service account|An EKS workload using IRSA receives an STS trust error; the role trust subject names a different namespace.|The role trust condition does not match the workload service-account subject.|Compare the projected identity issuer and subject with the role trust policy.|Correct the narrowly scoped trust subject for the intended service account.|Confirm the workload assumes only its intended role and can perform its required action.|Manage service-account identity and trust policy changes together.

Azure AKS|The forbidden registry|An AKS node can reach ACR but receives authorization denied while pulling a private image.|The cluster's effective image-pull identity lacks registry pull permission.|Identify the kubelet pull identity and inspect its effective registry permissions.|Grant the required registry pull permission to the correct managed identity.|Pull the image from a new workload on the affected node pool.|Manage registry access with the actual node pull identity and verify new pools.

Azure Key Vault|The inaccessible secret|A workload authenticates to Key Vault, but data-plane secret access is denied; no secret-reader role is assigned under RBAC mode.|Authentication succeeds but the identity lacks data-plane secret authorization.|Inspect the vault permission model and the workload's effective data-plane roles.|Assign the minimal required secret-read role at the appropriate scope.|Read the intended secret using the workload identity and verify denied operations stay denied.|Separate authentication checks from scoped data-plane authorization checks.

Azure Monitor|The empty workspace|An Azure VM runs its monitoring agent but no logs arrive; its data collection rule is not associated with the VM.|The agent has no applicable data collection rule association.|Inspect the agent status and effective data collection rule associations.|Associate the approved rule and destination workspace with the VM.|Confirm new records appear in the intended workspace with correct timestamps.|Manage collection rules and resource associations together as code.

Google GKE|The missing workload binding|A GKE pod obtains its Kubernetes identity but cannot impersonate the intended Google service account; the workload binding names another KSA.|The workload identity binding targets the wrong Kubernetes service account.|Inspect the cluster identity mode and the KSA-to-cloud-identity binding.|Correct the approved binding for the exact namespace and Kubernetes service account.|Run the required API operation from the intended pod without distributing service-account keys.|Version identity bindings with workload namespace and service-account configuration.

Google Artifact Registry|The wrong repository location|A pipeline pushes to a registry hostname in a different location from the configured repository and gets repository not found.|The image URL points to the wrong registry location.|Compare the image hostname and project/repository path with the actual repository location.|Use the exact regional repository URL and approved authentication configuration.|Push and pull an immutable test image at the intended repository path.|Generate registry image coordinates from reviewed environment configuration.

Kubernetes|The endless image pull|A pod has ImagePullBackOff; events report manifest unknown for a tag that the registry does not contain.|The deployment references an image tag absent from the registry.|Compare the pod image reference with available registry tags and digests.|Deploy the approved existing image digest or publish the missing intended artifact.|Confirm new pods pull the image and become Ready.|Verify image existence and deploy immutable digests before promotion.

Kubernetes|The overbooked citadel|Pods remain Pending; scheduler events report insufficient memory against requested resources.|The workload memory requests exceed available schedulable capacity.|Compare pod requests, node allocatable memory and current reservations.|Add approved capacity or right-size requests using measured workload needs.|Confirm pods schedule without overcommitting the intended resource budget.|Capacity-plan requests and test scheduling constraints before rollout.

Helm|The wrong release values|A Helm release uses the chart's default replica count; the pipeline omitted its production values file.|The production override file was not supplied during the release.|Inspect the Helm command and computed values for the release.|Render and review the release with the correct values file, then upgrade.|Inspect applied values and verify the intended replica count becomes Ready.|Version environment values and validate rendered manifests before release.

Argo CD|The permanent out-of-sync loop|Argo CD repeatedly reports drift because an operator mutates a specific generated annotation on every reconcile.|A controller-owned generated field differs from the desired manifest.|Inspect the exact diff and establish which controller owns the changing field.|Remove competing ownership or narrowly configure a justified field-level diff exception.|Confirm meaningful manifest changes still produce drift while the owned field no longer loops.|Define field ownership and review narrow diff exclusions instead of ignoring whole resources.

Flux|The unbuilt revision|Flux cannot build a Kustomization because spec.path references a directory removed in the latest Git revision.|The reconciler points to a nonexistent repository path.|Inspect the fetched source revision and the configured Kustomization path.|Correct the desired path in Git and reconcile the intended revision.|Confirm the reconciler reports Ready for the expected revision.|Validate GitOps source paths and builds in pull requests.

Kustomize|The surviving old image|Kustomize's image transformer names api, but the base image is registry.example/team/api, so the replacement is not applied.|The image transformer name does not match the base image name.|Inspect the base image reference and the rendered Kustomize output.|Set the transformer name to the matching base image name and render again.|Confirm the rendered and deployed image uses the approved new digest.|Validate rendered image references against release metadata in CI.

Prometheus|The vanished target|Prometheus marks a target down; the scrape path is /metrics but the exporter serves /prometheus.|The configured scrape path does not match the exporter endpoint.|Inspect the target scrape error and query the exporter endpoint from the scrape network.|Correct the scrape path for that target without weakening authentication.|Confirm up is one and expected metric series are scraped.|Define and validate exporter endpoint contracts with scrape configuration.

Grafana|The empty dashboard|A Grafana panel returns no series; the Prometheus metric exists but the panel filters namespace=prod while data uses production.|The dashboard label filter excludes the actual series.|Inspect the panel query and available label values in the data source.|Correct the reviewed label filter or variable mapping.|Confirm the panel shows the intended series over the selected time range.|Use consistent label conventions and validate dashboard variables against real data.

Alertmanager|The duplicate pages|Two Alertmanager instances send duplicate pages; mesh traffic between them is blocked after a firewall change.|Alertmanager peers cannot coordinate notification deduplication.|Inspect peer membership, connectivity and notification timing across replicas.|Restore the intended restricted peer-network connectivity.|Send a controlled alert and verify healthy peer membership and expected deduplication.|Monitor Alertmanager clustering and include peer ports in network policy reviews.

Grafana Loki|The exploding label set|Loki ingestion struggles after request_id is added as an indexed label with millions of unique values.|A high-cardinality request identifier creates excessive label streams.|Inspect stream counts and label cardinality changes in the ingestion configuration.|Remove the request identifier from indexed labels and retain it as structured metadata or log content.|Verify stream cardinality and ingestion errors fall while request details remain searchable.|Define label cardinality budgets and review new labels before ingestion changes.

Elasticsearch|The unassigned replica|A one-node Elasticsearch cluster is yellow; all primary shards are assigned and each index requests a replica.|Replica shards cannot be placed on the same node as their primary.|Inspect shard allocation explanations and the number of eligible nodes.|Add appropriate eligible capacity, or use zero replicas only where reduced redundancy is explicitly acceptable.|Confirm the intended shard placement and redundancy state match the environment design.|Align replica policy with node topology and durability requirements.

Logstash|The parsing dead end|Logstash tags every new access line with _grokparsefailure after the application log format changes.|The grok pattern no longer matches the emitted log format.|Compare representative raw log lines with the configured parser pattern.|Update and validate the parser against both supported old and new formats.|Confirm sample events parse into the expected fields without losing raw data.|Version log schemas and maintain parser samples for format migrations.

OpenTelemetry|The overloaded collector|An OpenTelemetry collector drops spans under peak traffic; exporter queues remain full and the backend is slow.|Telemetry export backpressure exceeds the collector's buffering capacity.|Inspect queue utilization, export latency, dropped spans and backend limits.|Reduce telemetry pressure or scale the constrained export path with bounded queues.|Confirm dropped-span rate and queue pressure recover during representative traffic.|Budget telemetry volume and monitor collector saturation and exporter failures.

Jaeger|The broken trace|An inbound HTTP span exists in Jaeger, but downstream spans have new trace IDs; outbound headers lack trace context.|Trace context is not propagated across the service boundary.|Inspect instrumentation and propagation headers on the outbound request.|Configure compatible context propagation in both services' instrumentation.|Follow one request end-to-end and confirm related spans share a trace.|Include cross-service trace continuity in observability checks.

Trivy|The unsigned scan result|A Trivy job finds critical vulnerabilities but the pipeline stays green because it leaves the exit code at zero.|The scan is informational and does not enforce the intended severity gate.|Inspect severity selection, ignore policy and scanner exit-code configuration.|Configure the reviewed severity gate and nonzero failure exit code with documented exceptions.|Scan a known failing fixture and confirm the deployment gate blocks it.|Version vulnerability gate policy and validate both allowed and rejected fixtures.

SonarQube|The unenforced gate|A SonarQube analysis completes with a failed quality gate, but deployment begins before the pipeline checks that result.|The pipeline submits analysis without waiting for or enforcing its quality gate.|Inspect the analysis task and the pipeline's quality-gate wait condition.|Add the supported quality-gate wait and fail the deployment path on rejection.|Submit a failing analysis and confirm deployment is blocked.|Treat quality-gate completion as an explicit dependency of release stages.

Snyk|The wrong dependency graph|Snyk scans a monorepo's root manifest, but the vulnerable service dependency lives in a nested project never scanned.|The configured scan scope omits the affected dependency project.|Compare repository project manifests with the scanner's detected and included projects.|Scan the intended nested manifests using the appropriate supported project discovery options.|Verify the vulnerable dependency appears in the affected service's scan result.|Maintain an inventory of scanned projects and check coverage when adding services.

Gitleaks|The leaked deployment token|Gitleaks finds a valid production token in a merged commit; deleting the current line does not invalidate it.|A live credential remains exposed in Git history.|Identify the credential owner, scope and exposure timeline without redistributing the secret.|Revoke or rotate the token immediately, then coordinate incident investigation and history cleanup.|Confirm the old token is rejected and the approved replacement works.|Use secret stores, short-lived credentials and secret scanning before merges.

Semgrep|The ignored security path|A Semgrep policy exists, but the CI include patterns exclude the service directory containing the unsafe call.|The security scan never analyzes the affected source path.|Inspect effective scan targets, ignore patterns and rule selection.|Include the affected source path under the intended security policy.|Use a representative rule fixture in that directory and confirm detection.|Validate scan coverage and exclusions when repository layouts change.

HashiCorp Vault|The expired lease|A service's dynamic database credentials stop working after lease expiry; its renewal agent has been down.|The service keeps using credentials whose Vault lease expired.|Inspect the credential lease, renewal attempts and agent health without logging secrets.|Restore the approved renewal flow and obtain fresh credentials for the service.|Confirm application access recovers and renewal occurs before the next lease expiry.|Monitor renewal failures and design applications to reload rotated credentials.

OPA Gatekeeper|The denied admission|Gatekeeper rejects a Deployment lacking the required owner label; the policy is scoped to its namespace.|The manifest violates the namespace's required metadata constraint.|Read the admission violation and the matching constraint and template.|Add the legitimate owner label to the version-controlled manifest.|Confirm the compliant manifest is admitted and the violating fixture remains rejected.|Validate policy compliance before deployment with representative manifests.

Kyverno|The unverified image|Kyverno rejects an image because its signature identity does not match the configured trusted build workflow.|The artifact is not signed by the policy's approved identity.|Inspect the verified signature identity, issuer, digest and matching policy.|Build and sign through the approved workflow or correct a reviewed trust-policy error.|Deploy the approved signed digest and confirm an untrusted fixture is still blocked.|Bind image trust to immutable digests and approved workflow identities.

Falco|The unexpected shell|Falco alerts on an interactive shell in a production container with no approved maintenance session.|An unexplained interactive shell requires incident investigation.|Correlate the container, user, exec audit event and authorized maintenance records.|Contain the affected workload under the incident procedure while preserving evidence.|Confirm the suspicious session is stopped and legitimate service health is assessed.|Restrict exec access, audit privileged actions and investigate runtime alerts.

Redis|The eviction storm|Redis uses all configured memory and evicts cache entries continuously; hit rate collapses after larger objects are introduced.|The cache working set exceeds its configured memory capacity.|Inspect memory use, eviction policy, key sizes and hit-rate changes.|Reduce unnecessary cache footprint or add approved capacity with a suitable eviction policy.|Confirm hit rate and evictions stabilize under representative load.|Budget cache item sizes, TTLs and memory with growth alerts.

PostgreSQL|The blocking migration|A PostgreSQL migration waits on an exclusive lock held behind a long-running transaction.|A long-running transaction blocks the schema migration's lock acquisition.|Inspect pg_stat_activity and pg_locks to identify the lock chain and transaction owner.|Coordinate safe completion or approved cancellation of the blocking transaction before the migration.|Confirm the lock is released and the migration and application transactions complete.|Use lock timeouts and rehearse compatible low-lock migration strategies.

MySQL|The slow replica|A MySQL replica lags after a bulk write; read routing sends freshness-sensitive requests to that replica.|Asynchronous replication has not caught up with the write workload.|Inspect replication lag, apply progress and the freshness requirement of affected reads.|Route freshness-sensitive reads to the appropriate consistent source while addressing apply capacity.|Verify the replica catches up and affected reads meet the required freshness.|Design read routing with explicit consistency and lag thresholds.

Apache Kafka|The rebalancing spiral|Kafka consumers exceed max.poll.interval while processing oversized batches; the group repeatedly rebalances.|Batch processing exceeds the consumer poll interval budget.|Compare processing time, poll timing and group rebalance events.|Bound batch processing and tune poll limits coherently with the workload.|Confirm stable group membership and falling consumer lag under representative load.|Load-test consumer processing budgets and alert on rebalance storms.

RabbitMQ|The unacked flood|RabbitMQ consumers use unlimited prefetch; a slow consumer accumulates many unacknowledged messages and runs out of memory.|Unbounded delivery prefetch overloads the slow consumer.|Inspect channel prefetch, unacknowledged count and consumer memory.|Set a bounded prefetch suited to processing capacity and acknowledge only after successful processing.|Confirm in-flight messages and memory stabilize without losing required delivery guarantees.|Use bounded concurrency, deliberate acknowledgement behavior and queue monitoring.

Kubernetes + PostgreSQL|The schema trap|A new release drops a database column; old pods still query it; rolling back the image reproduces missing-column errors.|An incompatible schema change breaks both old pods and image-only rollback.|Correlate schema migration history with old and new application query requirements.|Stabilize traffic with a schema-compatible application and an approved data-safe recovery plan.|Validate critical transactions across all remaining pod versions against the actual schema.|Use expand-contract migrations and verify rollback compatibility before destructive changes.

Terraform + AWS IAM|The locked recovery|A Terraform apply changes its own runner's IAM access and then loses backend write permission; state persistence fails after resources changed.|The apply revoked permissions needed to persist its resulting state.|Preserve local recovery state and audit actual resources, backend versions and changed permissions.|Restore authorized backend access, then reconcile preserved state through a reviewed recovery process.|Confirm a refreshed plan matches deployed resources with no unintended recreation.|Separate deployment-runner access from managed application permissions and test permission transitions.

Kubernetes + AWS ALB|The false green release|A rollout is Ready but the ALB returns errors; readiness checks a local stub while database authentication fails.|The readiness signal does not represent the application's required serving capability.|Correlate real request failures, database auth logs and readiness implementation.|Restore valid database access and deploy a meaningful bounded readiness contract.|Run representative requests through the ALB and confirm required dependencies behave correctly.|Define user-facing release checks alongside accurate readiness and rollback criteria.

Amazon Route 53 + RDS|The dangerous failover|Region A is network-isolated, not confirmed stopped; Region B's asynchronous replica lags; operators propose promoting B and sending writes to both.|Unfenced failover risks divergent writes and acknowledged-data loss.|Establish the old writer's fencing status, replication position and accepted RPO before promotion.|Fence the old writer and follow the approved data-loss-aware failover procedure to one writable primary.|Confirm one authoritative writer, required data consistency and end-to-end critical writes.|Rehearse regional failure with explicit fencing, RPO, RTO and reconciliation plans.

Argo CD + Helm|The healing rollback loop|An operator rolls back a Deployment manually; Argo CD self-heal immediately reapplies the bad image still recorded in Git.|The manual rollback conflicts with the GitOps source of truth.|Compare the live revision, Git desired digest and reconciliation settings.|Revert the desired image in Git or use the documented temporary reconciliation pause during recovery.|Confirm the healthy digest remains deployed through multiple reconciliation cycles.|Make rollback procedures update the desired source and record emergency pauses.

Prometheus + Alertmanager|The invisible outage|All applications in one zone disappear; a broad inhibition rule suppresses their alerts under a maintenance alert that was never cleared.|Overbroad stale maintenance inhibition hides an actual outage.|Inspect inhibition matches, maintenance lifecycle and independent service probes.|Remove or narrow the stale inhibition through incident control and restore independent paging.|Inject a controlled affected-service alert and verify the correct receiver is notified.|Use expiring scoped maintenance controls and independent alert-delivery checks.

Vault + Kubernetes|The cascading expiry|Vault is unavailable; pods retain usable credentials briefly, but a blanket restart destroys those pods before any replacement can fetch secrets.|Restarting healthy holders of valid credentials turns a secret outage into a service outage.|Inventory remaining credential lifetimes, running capacity and Vault recovery status.|Preserve serving capacity, restore Vault availability and rotate or restart in controlled batches.|Confirm new pods obtain valid credentials and old credentials retire safely without capacity loss.|Plan secret-service outages with bounded caching, renewal monitoring and staged recovery.

Kafka + PostgreSQL|The duplicate payment|A consumer commits a database payment then crashes before committing its Kafka offset; replay charges the same event again.|The database effect and consumer offset are not coordinated with idempotency.|Trace the event ID, transaction commit and offset position across the crash boundary.|Implement transactionally enforced event idempotency and reconcile duplicate side effects through the business recovery process.|Replay the same event across forced crash boundaries and confirm one business effect.|Use durable deduplication or an appropriate transaction/outbox design for cross-system delivery.

Redis + Kubernetes|The cache avalanche|A Redis restart empties a shared cache; every pod fetches the same expensive keys from an already saturated database.|A synchronized cache miss storm amplifies downstream load.|Correlate cache miss rate, duplicate key fetches and database saturation.|Bound cache refill concurrency, coalesce requests and shed noncritical work while warming safely.|Confirm backend load stays bounded and user latency recovers as the cache warms.|Use jittered TTLs, request coalescing and tested cold-cache capacity plans.
